report.tagline: A UK company that trains employees in data, AI and software skills through funded apprenticeships, paid for mostly by employers' apprenticeship levy.
report.simpleSummary: Multiverse runs work-based training programmes called apprenticeships. A person keeps doing their job, and spends about a fifth of their time learning skills like data analysis, AI or software engineering with Multiverse coaches and online classes. In the UK, big employers already pay a tax called the apprenticeship levy, and they can use it to pay Multiverse, so the training feels close to free for them. It started as an alternative to university for school leavers, and now mostly upskills existing staff in AI and data.

overview.whatItDoes: Multiverse sells training programmes to employers. Each programme is a government-approved apprenticeship standard, for example a Level 4 data analyst or AI and automation practitioner. Learners stay in their jobs, learn through live online workshops, coaching and self-paced content, and apply skills to real work projects. In the UK most of the cost is paid from the employer's levy pot, and in the US employers pay directly.
howItWorks: An employer signs up and picks programmes, for example data fundamentals or AI for business.
Employees apply, are checked for eligibility and join a cohort.
Learners spend about 20% of work time on off-the-job training: live sessions, online modules and work projects.
A Multiverse coach meets each learner regularly and tracks progress.
At the end, learners take an independent end-point assessment to earn the apprenticeship qualification.
The government releases levy funding to Multiverse in stages as the learner progresses.
overview.valueProposition: For employers: upskill staff in AI and data using money they already pay in levy. For learners: a recognised qualification and new skills without quitting work or taking on student debt.

painPoints.pain: Big UK employers pay the levy but often fail to spend it, so the money is lost.
painPoints.howSolved: Ready-made apprenticeship programmes that fit office jobs, so the levy turns into useful training.

painPoints.pain: Companies need AI and data skills quickly but cannot hire enough people.
painPoints.howSolved: Train existing staff in data and AI programmes built with partners such as Microsoft, Palantir and Databricks.

painPoints.pain: University is expensive and does not guarantee a job.
painPoints.howSolved: Learn while earning a salary, with no tuition debt.

painPoints.pain: Online courses have very low completion rates.
painPoints.howSolved: Human coaches, cohorts and work projects keep learners on track.

painPoints.pain: Apprenticeship rules and funding paperwork are complex.
painPoints.howSolved: Multiverse handles compliance, evidence and funding claims.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Structured 12 to 18 month programmes from Level 3 to Level 7 in data, AI, software and business.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: This is the product employers buy, and each programme maps to a government funding band.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: One-to-one coaches who check progress and help apply skills at work.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Keeps completion higher than self-paced courses; also the biggest cost.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Learners solve a real problem in their team as part of the course.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Lets employers see value, for example an automated report or saved hours.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: An AI assistant inside the platform that answers questions and gives feedback on work.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Supports learners between coach sessions and helps Multiverse grow without hiring as many coaches.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Shows enrolment, progress and outcomes across the company.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Helps training heads prove return on levy spend and renew.

businessModel.summary: Multiverse is paid per learner. In the UK, the money mostly comes from employers' apprenticeship levy accounts, with government funding bands setting the price. In the US, employers pay from their own training budgets.

revenueStreams.detail: The largest stream; apprenticeship training revenue was £58.9 million in 2023-24.
Companies pay directly for apprenticeship-style AI and data training.
Shorter AI skills programmes and partner-led courses sold to enterprises.

businessModel.pricing: Not public per customer. In the UK, prices follow government funding bands, which range up to about £25,000 for some data and AI standards; employers paying the levy usually pay nothing extra.
costDrivers: Coaches and instructors, the largest cost
businessModel.unitEconomics: Say one learner is on a data programme funded at about £15,000 to £20,000. Multiverse gets most of this in monthly instalments and a final payment on completion, so a learner who drops out earns less. Coaching time, instructors and sales take a big share of that money. With revenue of £79.6 million and a pre-tax loss of £63.3 million, Multiverse spent roughly £1.80 for every £1 it earned in 2024-25, so it loses money on its overall customer base today. It needs higher completion, more learners per coach and lower sales costs to break even.

howTheyGetUsers: Enterprise sales to levy-paying employers such as banks, councils and the NHS
Partnerships with Microsoft, Palantir and Databricks to co-brand AI programmes
Founder profile and press, including Euan Blair's public campaigning on apprenticeships
Internal spread: one successful cohort leads to more departments enrolling
whatBringsUsersBack: Employers' levy refills every month, so there is new money to spend
AI skills needs keep changing, so companies add new programmes
growth.moat: Multiverse knows how to turn the UK levy into AI training at scale, and it has the employer relationships, approved programmes and Ofsted track record to do it. A new rival needs years to build those. But much of that moat depends on government rules, which can change.

improvementIdeas.idea: AI coach handles routine progress reviews so human coaches cover more learners
improvementIdeas.problem: Coaching costs keep the company loss-making.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: More learners per coach without lower completion.

improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: New revenue that does not depend on levy rules.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Share of revenue from non-levy products

pmLessons: Find who already has budget. Multiverse grew by selling into money employers were already forced to spend.
When the government is your payer, policy changes are product risk. Plan for rules to change.
Completion is the product in education. Coaching costs money but makes the outcome real.
Follow demand: Multiverse moved from school leavers to AI upskilling for existing staff when that was what employers wanted.

interviewQuestions.question: Multiverse loses about £1.80 for every £1 earned. How would you get it to break even?
interviewQuestions.hint: Break cost into coaching, sales and platform. Look at learners per coach, completion rates, non-levy products and sales efficiency.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure whether a Multiverse apprenticeship worked for an employer?
interviewQuestions.hint: Separate learner outcomes (completion, promotion) from business outcomes (hours saved, projects shipped). Pick one north star.

interviewQuestions.question: The government cuts funding for one of Multiverse's biggest programmes. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Size the impact, protect current learners, test paid alternatives, move sales to funded programmes.

interviewQuestions.question: Design an AI feature for Multiverse learners.
interviewQuestions.hint: Pick one persona, one pain (time, generic content, feedback delay), define the AI behaviour and a completion metric.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Multiverse expand faster in the US, where there is no levy?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare willingness to pay, sales cycle, competitors and how the product must change without government funding.
